From half a mile away, Jake Molina sees a biography where most of us see a brown blur. Instead, he reads ear notches, horn shapes, and seasonal behavior, proving that patient on-the-ground knowledge still beats technology for understanding wild herds.

stories.extended_summary: For months, Chester resident Josh Johnson and his brother have been secretly building a network of low-frequency radio repeaters — and one of them was mistaken for a surveillance camera. stories.summary: Jack and the Bean is a Kenova nonprofit coffee shop with a mission: boost employment for people with developmental and intellectual disabilities. stories.extended_summary: Melanie Adkins didn't say her first words until he was three — and now he's the heart of a coffee shop with a mission. When Jack approached high school graduation, his mom started thinking about adulthood and landed on an on-the-go coffee stand they could run together. Their first gig was a Christmas play concession stand, and it proved they could handle it. About a year later, Jack and the Bean connected with Diversified Assessment Therapy Systems, which provides job training for people with developmental and intellectual disabilities, and the nonprofit coffee shop was born. It's open every Wednesday from 6 to 10 a.m. in Kenova, serving coffee and community to everyone.

stories.extended_summary: "It's the most basic technology out there." That's Ansel Troy's message to anyone who thinks solar is only for the pros. The East Oakland tinkerer has been documenting his backyard experiments on Instagram (@tinyoakland), showing viewers where to buy plug-in units, whether a battery is worth it, and how to set everything up safely. His timing is perfect: in September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law allowing 1.2-kilowatt plug-in solar devices without utility permits or extra fees. Troy's growing audience is hungry for practical advice, and his videos make clean energy feel less like magic and more like something you could actually do this weekend.

stories.summary: A new project called The Golden Thread is marking East Boston's immigrant history with five gold-hued steel arches across the neighborhood — starting at the Golden Stairs, where thousands of newcomers took their first steps in America a century ago.
stories.extended_summary: Fifty-eight concrete stairs rise from East Boston's Marginal Street — a century ago, thousands of immigrants climbed them from the piers below as their first steps on American soil. Now a gold-hued metal arch called 'Arrival' crowns the ascent, the first of five 'thresholds' in creator David Lank's Golden Thread cultural trail. The arches celebrate the neighborhood's cultural, maritime and infrastructure roots, hosted by Massport, the City of Boston and local groups. 'It's actually a neighborhood story,' Lank says, 'and how that story does already exist, but it's still being written.'

stories.title: ‘We Deserve It’: In Birmingham, Black Farmers Open Fountain Heights’ First Grocery Store in 70 years
stories.summary: Birmingham's Fountain Heights neighborhood just got its first grocery store in nearly 70 years. A Black-owned farming cooperative opened We All Eat Market, stocked with fresh produce from their own plots — and the whole community showed up to celebrate.
stories.extended_summary: For nearly 70 years, residents of Birmingham's Fountain Heights had no grocery store of their own. That changed on Nov. 7, when the Fountain Heights Farms Cooperative — a Black-owned urban farm founded in 2016 — threw open the doors of We All Eat Market. Shelves lined with bulk grains, fresh juice, and herbs grown by co-founder Christopher Gooden sit beside a produce stand stocked from the collective's own plots and farms across Alabama. The grand opening felt like a block party: hugs, cooking demos, and neighbors finally shopping close to home. "We deserve it," the community said — and now they've built it.
